title: ISAAC PRAYED FOR HIS INFERTILE WIFE—AND GOD ANSWERED WITH TWINS: THE MIRACLE THAT CAME AFTER 20 YEARS OF WAITING
paragraphs: ISAAC PRAYED FOR HIS INFERTILE WIFE—AND GOD ANSWERED WITH TWINS: THE MIRACLE THAT CAME AFTER 20 YEARS OF WAITING

She carried the heartbreak of an empty womb. He carried a promise from God. For twenty years, nothing changed—until a husband's prayer became part of a story that would shape generations. But the most powerful revelation isn't that Rebekah became pregnant with twins. It's what God was doing while they waited.
There is a kind of pain that becomes harder to explain the longer you carry it.
At first, people ask questions because they care.
Then the questions become uncomfortable.
Then you begin avoiding certain conversations because you already know what someone is going to ask.
“Any good news yet?”
“Have you tried something different?”
“Maybe this will finally be your year.”
And you smile.
Because explaining the same heartbreak over and over again is exhausting.
But when you get home, when the door closes, when nobody is watching, the smile disappears.
You sit quietly.
And somewhere inside your heart, a question rises that you almost feel guilty asking.
“Lord, have You forgotten me?”
Maybe your struggle isn't infertility.
Maybe it's a marriage that feels like it's slowly dying.
A child who no longer wants anything to do with God.
A financial burden that follows you into your sleep.
A diagnosis you never expected.
A prayer you have whispered so many times that the words now come out through tears.
You believe God can answer.
You just don't understand why He hasn't.
And that's what makes the story of Isaac and Rebekah so painfully beautiful.
Because Genesis 25 doesn't introduce us to a man who didn't know God.
It introduces us to a man who inherited a promise from God.
Yet even with that promise, he and his wife endured years of unanswered longing.
Read that again.
Being connected to God's promise did not exempt them from the pain of waiting.
Isaac was the son of Abraham.
The child whose very existence was evidence that God could accomplish what human circumstances made impossible.
His mother, Sarah, had conceived him in her old age after years of barrenness.
Isaac grew up as living testimony that God keeps His word.
And then he married Rebekah.
A woman he loved.
A woman who would become part of God's covenant story.
A woman whose womb remained closed.
Can you imagine the emotional weight of that?
Isaac had been born because God overcame his mother's barrenness.
Now he was standing beside his own wife, facing a painfully familiar struggle.
The son of a miracle was waiting for another miracle.
And Scripture gives us one of the most tender glimpses into their marriage.
Genesis 25:21 says in the King James Version:
“And Isaac intreated the LORD for his wife, because she was barren: and the LORD was intreated of him, and Rebekah his wife conceived.”
There is something extraordinary hidden inside that seemingly simple verse.
Isaac didn't merely acknowledge his wife's suffering.
He brought it before God.
He didn't treat her infertility as a reason to abandon her.
He prayed for her.
And if you've ever carried a burden that seemed too heavy to explain, you understand how precious it is when someone refuses to leave you alone in your suffering.
Someone who doesn't pretend to have all the answers.
Someone who doesn't offer another empty explanation.
Someone who simply says, “I am going to pray with you.”
But there is an even deeper beauty in the original Hebrew.
The verse begins:
וַיֶּעְתַּר יִצְחָק לַיהוָה לְנֹכַח אִשְׁתּוֹ
Vayye'tar Yitschaq la-YHWH lenokhach ishto.
A careful rendering is:
“And Isaac pleaded with the LORD on behalf of his wife.”
The Hebrew verb וַיֶּעְתַּר (vayye'tar) comes from the root עתר (ʿ-t-r), used here for earnest supplication or entreaty.
This was prayer directed toward the living God.
Not a magical formula.
Not an attempt to control heaven.
Not a transaction in which Isaac offered enough religious effort to force a blessing.
It was petition.
Dependence.
A husband bringing a need beyond his power to the God whose power was not limited by that need.

The expression לְנֹכַח אִשְׁתּוֹ (lenokhach ishto) has the sense of “on behalf of his wife” or “in relation to his wife.” Some interpreters understand it as suggesting that Isaac prayed in her presence or opposite her, but the verse does not explicitly describe their physical posture.
We should not invent a scene Scripture does not give us.
Yet what Scripture does reveal is powerful enough.
Isaac interceded for Rebekah.
And God heard.
The second half of the verse says:
וַיֵּעָתֶר לוֹ יְהוָה
Vayye'ater lo YHWH.
“And the LORD responded to his plea.”
The Hebrew deliberately echoes the language of Isaac's entreaty.
Isaac pleaded.
The LORD responded.
The same root connects the human petition with the divine answer.
That is beautiful.
But before you rush toward the miracle, you need to see something that makes this story even more astonishing.
Genesis 25:20 tells us Isaac was forty years old when he married Rebekah.
Genesis 25:26 tells us he was sixty when Esau and Jacob were born.
Twenty years.
Twenty years between marriage and the birth of their children.
Scripture does not tell us exactly when Isaac began praying or how frequently he prayed during those years. It does tell us that Rebekah was barren, that Isaac prayed for her, and that God answered.
And those twenty years matter.
Because we sometimes read biblical miracles as if they happened within a few paragraphs of ordinary life.
One verse says there was a problem.
The next verse announces the answer.
And we turn the page without feeling the years between them.
But Rebekah had to live those years.
Isaac had to live those years.
Twenty years of ordinary mornings.
Twenty years of family gatherings.
Twenty years of wondering what the future would look like.
Twenty years in which the covenant promise was still true, even though the circumstances looked painfully unresolved.
Perhaps you've been waiting so long that you no longer tell people what you're praying for.
You don't want another disappointed conversation.
You don't want to explain why the answer hasn't come.
You don't want to hear someone suggest that your faith must be too weak.
And maybe the hardest part is watching other people receive what you've been asking God for.
You celebrate with them.
You mean it.
But sometimes, after the celebration, you go somewhere quiet and cry.
If that's you, please hear this carefully.
An unanswered prayer is not proof that God has rejected you.
And a delayed answer is not automatically evidence that you have failed spiritually.
Isaac's story does not teach that every couple experiencing infertility will conceive if they pray long enough.
It does not teach that infertility is punishment.
It does not teach that having children is the measure of a person's worth, holiness, or standing before God.
Those conclusions would wound people whom Scripture never gives us permission to condemn.
The Bible tells us what God did for Isaac and Rebekah within His particular covenant purposes.
It does not give us authority to promise every believer the same earthly outcome.
And that distinction matters because people are not illustrations to be used carelessly.
They are souls Jesus loves.
Some people will read this while holding a newborn.
Others will read it after another negative pregnancy test.
Some are still hoping.
Some have experienced miscarriage.
Some have buried dreams they can barely speak about.
Some have come to understand that their lives may unfold differently than they once imagined.
And the Gospel must be good news for all of them.
Not only for the person whose circumstances change.
But also for the person who is still waiting.
Because the greatest gift God gives us is not a particular earthly outcome.
It is Himself, through Jesus Christ.
And this is where Isaac's story begins to open into something much bigger than the miracle of conception.
Because when Rebekah finally became pregnant, the story did not suddenly become easy.
Genesis 25:22 says:
“And the children struggled together within her; and she said, If it be so, why am I thus? And she went to enquire of the LORD.”
Imagine that.
The woman who had longed for a child was now carrying children.
But instead of uninterrupted peace, she experienced troubling movement within her womb.
The Hebrew describes the children struggling against one another.
The verb is unusually forceful, conveying intense internal conflict.
Rebekah didn't know what was happening.
She had received what she had long desired, yet now she faced another frightening question.
And notice what she did.
She went to inquire of the LORD.
Isaac prayed when she could not conceive.
Rebekah sought God when she could not understand what was happening inside her.
This is not merely a story about a praying husband.
It is also a story about a woman who sought the Lord for herself.
There is dignity in that.
There is spiritual agency in that.
There is a reminder that God was not dealing only with Isaac while Rebekah stood silently in the background.
The LORD spoke concerning the children she carried.
Genesis 25:23 records His answer:
“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.”
Two nations.
Not simply two babies.
Two peoples whose histories would become intertwined with conflict.
Esau and Jacob.
Edom and Israel.
And suddenly, what had looked like one family's private heartbreak was revealed to be part of a much larger covenant story.
Rebekah was carrying twins.
But the twins would not have an uncomplicated relationship.
The children would struggle.
The brothers would clash.
The family would experience favoritism, deception, broken trust, separation, and grief.
God's answer to Isaac's prayer did not mean their family would be free from trouble.
That truth may be one of the most important things in this entire account.
A blessing from God does not mean every chapter afterward will be painless.
Sometimes we imagine that if God would only answer one particular prayer, everything else would finally fall into place.
If the marriage were restored, we'd never struggle again.
If the debt disappeared, we'd never be afraid again.
If the medical report changed, we'd never question again.
If the child returned home, our hearts would never break again.
But life is more complicated than that.
And the Bible is too honest to pretend otherwise.
Isaac and Rebekah received children.
They also entered a story filled with human weakness.
Genesis 25:28 tells us Isaac loved Esau because of his taste for wild game, while Rebekah loved Jacob.
Favoritism took root.
Later, in Genesis 27, Rebekah and Jacob deceived Isaac so that Jacob would receive the blessing Isaac intended to give Esau.
The family that had experienced divine intervention also experienced profound dysfunction.
This is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes impossible to ignore.
Because Jacob was not a flawless hero.
He was a complicated man.
A man who would deceive and be deceived.
A man who would run.
A man who would wrestle.
A man whose life would expose how deeply human beings need the mercy of God.
And yet God did not abandon His covenant purposes.
In Genesis 32, Jacob wrestled through the night and received the name Israel.
The man who once fled from his brother would eventually meet him again.
And in Genesis 33, we see a remarkable scene of reconciliation.
Esau ran to meet Jacob.
He embraced him.
He fell on his neck and kissed him.
And they wept.
Two brothers.
Once divided by betrayal.
Now standing face to face.
Their later histories would remain complicated, but that moment of reconciliation is unmistakably moving.
The twins Isaac had prayed for were not merely the ending of one painful season.
Their lives became part of a story revealing human sin, divine faithfulness, judgment, mercy, and the extraordinary patience of God.
And through Jacob's descendants, the story would eventually lead us to Jesus Christ.
This is the point where we must be careful not to miss the center of Scripture.
The greatest significance of Isaac's family is not that their experience gives us a guaranteed formula for receiving miracles.
It is that God preserved His covenant promise through a deeply imperfect family.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Generations of people who were never righteous enough to save themselves.
And eventually, through the lineage of Israel, came Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:2 begins the genealogy this way:
“Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren.”
That “Judas” is the King James rendering of Judah.
And Matthew traces the family line forward until we arrive at Jesus, who is called Christ.
Do you see what is happening?
The Lord who answered Isaac's prayer was carrying forward a promise that would ultimately find its fulfillment in the Messiah.
Not because every person in that family behaved perfectly.
They didn't.
Not because the family had no scandals.
They did.
Not because human beings consistently remained faithful.
They didn't.
But because God is faithful.
And His redemptive purposes are not defeated by human failure.
The apostle Paul reflects on the significance of Isaac and Rebekah's children in Romans 9:10–13, emphasizing God's sovereign purpose rather than human merit.

That passage raises profound theological questions, but one truth stands clearly within its argument: God's saving purpose is not something sinful humanity can earn through achievement or moral superiority.
And that should humble every one of us.
Because some of us have spent years trying to become worthy of God's love.
We pray.
We serve.
We give.
We attend church.
We try to make fewer mistakes.
And somewhere along the way, without realizing it, we begin to treat our relationship with God like a negotiation.
“Lord, I've done so much. Why haven't You answered?”
“Lord, I've been faithful. Why is this happening?”
“Lord, I've given You everything. What more do You want?”
But the Gospel does not begin with what we can offer God.
It begins with what God has given us in Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we finally became impressive.
Not after we learned how to pray without distraction or doubt.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And if you've ever wondered whether your past has disqualified you from grace, look at the family through which the Messiah came.
There were lies.
There was manipulation.
There was sexual sin.
There was violence.
There was failure.
There were consequences that could not simply be erased.
Yet the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that God's redemptive plan moved through a world full of broken people.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Jesus did not come to celebrate our scandals. He came to save sinners and transform lives.
He came calling people to repentance.
He came offering forgiveness.
He came to reconcile us to the Father.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He died for our sins.
And He rose again, defeating death.
The empty tomb is greater than an empty womb becoming fruitful.
Not because Isaac and Rebekah's suffering was insignificant.
But because the resurrection of Jesus Christ is the decisive victory upon which our eternal hope rests.
An answered prayer can change a season of life.
The risen Christ can give us eternal life.
And perhaps that's the revelation your heart needs most today.
You have been asking God to change something around you.
But the deepest need of every human soul is to be reconciled to the God who made us.
Maybe you've been praying for a miracle while secretly drifting away from Jesus.
Maybe disappointment has made your heart bitter.
Maybe you've been comparing your life to everyone else's until gratitude has almost disappeared.
Maybe you still attend church, but your private life tells a different story.
Maybe there is a sin you've been protecting.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A resentment you refuse to surrender.
A habit you keep promising to abandon.
A secret you hope nobody discovers.
And now you're reading about Isaac's prayer, but something deeper is stirring.
Because the question is no longer only, “Will God give me what I've been asking for?”
It has become, “Lord, what is happening to my heart while I wait?”
That's a question worth facing.
Not with shame that drives you away from God.
But with godly sorrow that leads you toward repentance.
Second Corinthians 7:10 teaches that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation.
And 1 John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and just to forgive sins when we confess them.
You don't have to pretend in the presence of the One who already knows you completely.
You don't have to manufacture a testimony that sounds impressive.
You don't have to claim a miracle that hasn't happened.
You can come to Jesus with the truth.
“Lord, I'm tired.”
“Lord, I'm disappointed.”
“Lord, I'm struggling to trust You.”
“Lord, I've sinned.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
“Lord, help my unbelief.”
That last prayer echoes the desperate father in Mark 9:24:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
What a painfully human confession.
Faith and weakness in the same sentence.
Belief and struggle in the same heart.
And Jesus did not demand that the father pretend his faith was flawless.
Maybe you've needed permission to stop pretending.
Not permission to abandon faith.
But permission to bring your weakness honestly before Christ.
Because genuine faith does not require you to deny your pain.
It calls you to entrust yourself to God in the middle of it.
And there is another detail in Isaac's story that deserves our attention.
Isaac's name in Hebrew is יִצְחָק (Yitschaq), connected to the verb meaning “to laugh.”
His name reaches back to the astonishing promise of his birth.
Abraham and Sarah had encountered a promise so extraordinary that laughter became part of the story.
Genesis 21:6 records Sarah saying:
“God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me.”
Isaac's very name carried the memory of God's faithfulness.
Yet the man whose name was associated with laughter would himself experience a long season of waiting.
Isn't that remarkable?
A person can carry testimony from yesterday and still face uncertainty tomorrow.
You can have seen God provide before and still tremble when the next bill arrives.
You can have witnessed healing in someone else's life and still struggle with your own suffering.
You can know Scripture and still cry.
You can love Jesus and still have questions.
The existence of questions does not automatically mean the absence of faith.
And the presence of tears does not mean the absence of God's love.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
That promise does not mean every broken circumstance will immediately be repaired.
It means the brokenhearted are not beyond the Lord's care.
Perhaps you have spent years interpreting God's silence as rejection.
Perhaps you have looked at someone else's blessing and concluded that heaven must love them more.
But Isaac and Rebekah's story gives us no reason to measure divine love by the speed of an answer.
And the cross gives us a far greater reason to trust the heart of God.
Romans 8:32 asks:
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?”
Read that verse in its context.
Paul is not promising that believers will receive every earthly desire.
He is assuring God's people that nothing can ultimately defeat the saving love revealed in Jesus Christ.
Later in that same chapter, he speaks of tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword.
The love of Christ is not proved by the absence of suffering.
It is proved by His faithfulness even through suffering.
That changes how we pray.
We can still ask boldly.
We can still bring our needs before the Father.
We can still seek medical help, wise counsel, reconciliation, provision, and healing.
We can still pray for children.
For marriages.
For families.
For restoration.
But we pray as children approaching a loving Father, not customers attempting to purchase a result.
And we learn to say, as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42)
Those words are not spiritual defeat.
They are surrendered trust.
And sometimes surrender is the bravest prayer a person can pray.
“Father, I know what I want. You know how much it means to me. I am asking You with all my heart. But even if the road looks different from what I imagined, do not let me lose my grip on Jesus.”
If you're reading this with tears in your eyes, I want you to know something.
You do not need to turn your suffering into a performance for other people.
You do not need to pretend you're stronger than you are.
You do not need to force a happy ending onto a chapter that is still painful.
Bring the real story to God.
And if this message has uncovered something you've been carrying silently, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Not because commenting will unlock a miracle.
Not because public confession earns God's attention.
But because sometimes a simple, honest sentence can help another believer know they are not suffering alone.
And if your struggle is private, you do not have to disclose details. God hears the prayers you cannot safely or comfortably share online.
And if this story has exposed an area where you need to repent, you can write “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not as a formula.
Not as a public performance of holiness.
But as a sincere expression of a heart turning toward Christ.
Maybe someone reading the comments will find the courage to pray again.
Maybe someone will see that other believers wrestle with fear too.
Maybe someone who has quietly walked away from church will realize there is still a place for honest questions and genuine repentance.
That is the kind of community we want to cultivate through Gospel Warrior.
Not a gathering of people pretending to be perfect.
But a fellowship of people who know they need Jesus.
People who open their Bibles.
People who are willing to be corrected by Scripture.
People who encourage the weary.
People who refuse to confuse popularity with truth.
People who understand that real transformation comes through the Gospel, not through emotional excitement alone.
Not simply because sharing increases reach.
But because someone in your circle may be carrying a burden they've never told you about.
A cousin longing for a child.
A married couple who are struggling.
A father praying for his family.
A young believer who thinks unanswered prayer means God has abandoned them.
A friend who is slowly losing hope.
You may never know who reads a message you share in the quiet hours of the night.
But a Scripture-centered word, shared with love, can become an opportunity for someone to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Because there may come another night when you need to remember that the Bible never promised an easy life, but it does reveal a faithful Savior.
There is a reason we keep returning to the Word of God.
Human encouragement can comfort us for a moment.
But the truth of Scripture gives us something deeper to stand upon.
Jesus said in John 17:17:
“Sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth.”
That is the foundation of what we're building.
And I want to speak for a moment to those who have been strengthened by this ministry and have wondered how they can help it continue.
Our desire is to build a growing place of biblical encouragement, spiritual nourishment, repentance, healing, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our commitment to making Christian learning and spiritual growth more accessible.
And that work requires time, effort, stewardship, and ongoing support.
It helps sustain the work of producing Scripture-centered content and growing the resources we hope will serve more people.
And there is something important I want to make clear.
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.
You do not have to give money to make your prayers more effective.
Salvation is the gift of God through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial giving (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Biblical generosity must never be confused with buying God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
We encourage you to honor those responsibilities first.
Not as payment for spiritual privileges.
But as partnership in work intended to point people toward Jesus.
Those items can be meaningful reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, or resources for personal growth.
But the heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is making room for more people to read Scripture, confront sin, discover grace, and grow in Christ.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can engage in honest, Scripture-centered conversations.
You can encourage a struggling believer.
You can tell someone what Jesus has done in your life.
And you can help us keep the focus where it belongs.
On Christ.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus Christ known.
That is what matters.
And now, before we leave Isaac and Rebekah, I want you to notice something that may change the way you remember this story forever.
Isaac prayed for his wife.
God answered.
Rebekah conceived twins.
But neither Isaac nor Rebekah lived to see the entire redemptive story that would unfold through their descendants.
They did not stand in Bethlehem when Jesus was born.
They did not hear the crowds crying out as He entered Jerusalem.
They did not watch Him carry the cross to Golgotha.
They did not stand at the empty tomb on resurrection morning.
Yet the covenant promise God was preserving through their family would ultimately lead to the coming of the Savior.
Their understanding was limited.
God's purposes were greater than what they could see.
And that is where this story speaks so deeply to us.
We want to understand everything now.
Why the delay happened.
Why the door closed.
Why the relationship failed.
Why the answer came differently than we expected.
Why someone else received what we desperately wanted.
But Scripture does not promise that we will understand every mystery in this lifetime.
Deuteronomy 29:29 reminds us that secret things belong to the LORD, while what He has revealed belongs to us.
And what has He revealed?
That He is holy.
That sin is serious.
That His mercy is real.
That His promises are trustworthy.
That Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
That everyone who comes to Christ in genuine faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
And that nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him (Romans 8:38–39).
Perhaps that is enough truth to hold onto tonight.
You may not know when your circumstances will change.
You may not know whether the answer will look like the one you imagined.
You may not know why this particular season has lasted so long.
But you can know where to bring your heart.
To Jesus.
The Savior who understands suffering.
The High Priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses.
The Redeemer who does not turn away repentant sinners.
The risen Lord whose grace is greater than our shame.
And if your story includes a scandal, a failure, a painful decision, or a chapter you wish you could erase, remember that God's grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the mercy that calls you out of darkness.
Repentance matters.
Truth matters.
Holiness matters.
Forgiveness matters.
And in Christ, a person's past does not have to become the final definition of their future.
This is not because every earthly consequence disappears.
It is because Jesus offers a deeper redemption than mere reputation repair.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is the transformation worth longing for.
Not merely a changed situation.
But a life made new through Jesus Christ.
So tonight, if you're still waiting, pray.
If you're grieving, bring your tears.
If you've sinned, repent.
If you've wandered, return.
If you're confused, open the Scriptures.
If you're weary, ask a trusted believer to walk beside you.
If you need professional medical or emotional support, seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
And if you've never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, do not mistake religious activity for reconciliation with God.
Turn to Him.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive the grace you could never earn.
Follow Him.
Not because He has promised to make every earthly dream come true.
But because He is worthy.
Because He is Lord.
Because He is Savior.
Because even when life does not unfold the way you hoped, the Gospel remains true.
And maybe, one day, you will look back at a season that nearly broke you and realize that although you never understood everything, Christ was teaching you to depend on Him.
Not every waiting season ends with twins.
Not every prayer ends with the outcome we desire.
But every believer can rest in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And the God who carried His covenant promise through Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and generations of deeply imperfect people has not lost His power to redeem.
But above all, do not leave this story merely admiring Isaac's prayer.
Leave it looking to Isaac's God.
Leave it trusting Jesus.
Leave it remembering that the greatest miracle in the Christian life is not simply receiving something we thought was impossible.
It is being rescued from sin and brought into eternal life through the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you have one final prayer left in your exhausted heart, let it be this:

“Lord Jesus, whether You change my circumstances today or teach me to endure them faithfully, do not let my pain pull me away from You. Forgive my sins, restore my heart, strengthen my faith, and make my life a testimony of Your grace. Amen.”
Because the most unforgettable truth in Isaac and Rebekah's story is not simply that God gave them two sons after twenty years.
It is that God's covenant faithfulness continued through a family that desperately needed His grace.
And that same story ultimately points us to the Savior who is greater than every earthly miracle.
You may still be waiting for God to rewrite the chapter you're living, but at the cross, Jesus has already written the only ending that can save your soul.
